---
title: "NAF — Single-level classification"
---

## Hyperparameter sweep

The model predicts only the finest-grained **sub-class** code (679 classes in the training split) directly, in a single pass, with no auxiliary hierarchy levels — this is the baseline the [Multi-level classification](naf_multilevel.qmd) page is compared against.

The `naf` MLflow experiment mixes runs from three different `train_fraction` sweeps over the same hyperparameter grid: an earlier one at **0.13** (163,615 examples), a later one at **0.26** (314,230 examples), and the latest, largest one at **0.52** (628,461 examples). The corpus itself has 2.3M observations, but only ~1.3M carry a cleaned `libelle` usable as model input — `train_fraction` is taken against that ~1.3M subset, not the raw 2.3M. The rest of this section uses **0.52** only (the largest, most recent sweep) — the figure below is the exception, comparing all three to isolate the effect of training-data size itself.

```{python}
#| label: fetch-mlflow-naf

from pathlib import Path
import mlflow
import pandas as pd

RENAME_COLS = {
    "params.emb_dim":                  "emb_dim",
    "params.n_layers":                 "n_layers",
    "params.n_head":                   "n_head",
    "params.n_heads_label_attention":  "n_heads_label_attn",
    "params.vocab_size":               "vocab_size",
    "params.lr":                       "lr",
    "metrics.num_params":              "num_params",
    "metrics.test_accuracy":           "test_accuracy",
    "metrics.test_f1_macro":           "test_f1_macro",
    "metrics.train_time_s":            "train_time_s",
    "metrics.val_loss":                "min_val_loss",
}
KEY_COLS = ["n_layers", "emb_dim", "vocab_size", "n_head", "n_heads_label_attn", "lr"]

def arch_label(row):
    la = str(row["n_heads_label_attn"]) == "4"
    if row["n_layers"] == 0:
        return "FastText + Label Attention" if la else "FastText"
    suffix = " + Label Attention" if la else ""
    return f"FATE (L={row['n_layers']}){suffix}"

def fetch_runs(experiment_name: str, cache_path: Path, train_fraction: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
    cache_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    if cache_path.exists():
        return pd.read_csv(cache_path)
    raw = mlflow.search_runs(experiment_names=[experiment_name], max_results=5000)
    raw = raw[raw["status"] == "FINISHED"].copy()
    raw = raw[pd.to_numeric(raw["params.train_fraction"], errors="coerce") == train_fraction]
    raw = raw.rename(columns={k: v for k, v in RENAME_COLS.items() if k in raw.columns})
    for col in ["emb_dim", "n_layers", "vocab_size"]:
        raw[col] = pd.to_numeric(raw[col], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
    raw["lr"]         = raw["lr"].astype(float)
    raw["num_params"] = pd.to_numeric(raw["num_params"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
    raw["architecture"] = raw.apply(arch_label, axis=1)
    raw = raw.sort_values("min_val_loss").drop_duplicates(subset=KEY_COLS, keep="first")
    raw.to_csv(cache_path, index=False)
    return raw

# train_fraction=0.13 — earliest, smallest sweep
df_frac13 = fetch_runs("naf", Path("results/naf/runs_frac13.csv"), train_fraction=0.13)

# train_fraction=0.26 — intermediate sweep
df_frac26 = fetch_runs("naf", Path("results/naf/runs_frac26.csv"), train_fraction=0.26)

# train_fraction=0.52 — latest, largest sweep — used as the main dataset below
df_frac52 = fetch_runs("naf", Path("results/naf/runs_frac52.csv"), train_fraction=0.52)

df = df_frac52
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-trainsize-naf
#| fig-cap: "Validation loss vs. training set size, by architecture"

import plotly.graph_objects as go

COLORS = {
    "FastText":                          "#2196F3",
    "FastText + Label Attention":        "#00BCD4",
}
N_TRAIN = {0.13: 163615, 0.26: 314230, 0.52: 628461}

common_archs = ["FastText", "FastText + Label Attention"]
means13 = df_frac13[df_frac13["architecture"].isin(common_archs)].groupby("architecture")["min_val_loss"].mean()
means26 = df_frac26[df_frac26["architecture"].isin(common_archs)].groupby("architecture")["min_val_loss"].mean()
means52 = df_frac52[df_frac52["architecture"].isin(common_archs)].groupby("architecture")["min_val_loss"].mean()

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in common_archs:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[N_TRAIN[0.13], N_TRAIN[0.26], N_TRAIN[0.52]],
        y=[means13[arch], means26[arch], means52[arch]],
        mode="lines+markers", name=arch,
        line=dict(color=COLORS[arch], width=2), marker=dict(size=9),
        hovertemplate="train size=%{x:,}<br>mean val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Training set size", yaxis_title="Mean validation loss",
    xaxis=dict(
        tickvals=[N_TRAIN[0.13], N_TRAIN[0.26], N_TRAIN[0.52]],
        ticktext=["163,615", "314,230", "628,461"],
    ),
    legend_title="Architecture", height=430,
)
fig.show()
```

Growing the training data (163,615 → 314,230 → 628,461 examples) steadily improves mean validation loss for both architectures — FastText from ≈0.63 to ≈0.57 to ≈0.51, FastText + Label Attention from ≈0.76 to ≈0.63 to ≈0.53 — with the label-attention variant benefiting more at each step, consistent with it needing more examples per class to learn meaningful per-class query vectors; the gap between the two architectures narrows from ≈0.13 at 163,615 examples to ≈0.02 at 628,461.

### Capacity & robustness

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Val loss vs. parameters

```{python}
#| label: fig-pareto-naf
#| fig-cap: "Validation loss vs. number of parameters"

import plotly.graph_objects as go

COLORS = {
    "FastText":                          "#2196F3",
    "FastText + Label Attention":        "#00BCD4",
    "FATE (L=1)":                        "#FFC107",
    "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention":      "#FF8C00",
}
ARCHS_PRESENT = [a for a in COLORS if a in df["architecture"].unique()]

df_curves = (
    df.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size", "num_params"], as_index=False)
    ["min_val_loss"].min()
    .sort_values("num_params")
)

fig = go.Figure()

for arch in ARCHS_PRESENT:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=True,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS[arch], size=8, opacity=1.0),
    ))

for arch, group in df.groupby("architecture"):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["num_params"], y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), size=5, opacity=0.3),
        hovertemplate="params=%{x:,}<br>val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

for arch, group in df_curves.groupby("architecture"):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["num_params"], y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="lines+markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        line=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), width=2), marker=dict(size=5),
        hovertemplate="params=%{x:,}<br>best val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

y_cap = df["min_val_loss"].quantile(0.95)
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of parameters",
    yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    legend_title="Architecture",
    height=450,
    xaxis=dict(tickformat=".2s"),
    yaxis=dict(range=[df["min_val_loss"].min() * 0.98, y_cap]),
)
fig.show()
```

There's no clean pareto frontier here — loss doesn't fall monotonically with parameter count, since `num_params` mixes together several hyperparameters (vocabulary size, embedding dimension) whose individual effects pull in different directions. The figures further down break each one out separately to make sense of the zigzag.

Label attention consistently **hurts** across this whole grid, mirroring CLINC150 rather than Amazon, but the gap is far narrower here (mean val loss ≈0.51 for FastText vs. ≈0.53 for FastText + Label Attention, compared to a 2–4× gap on CLINC150). With ~630k training examples (`train_fraction=0.52` of the ~1.3M cleaned-`libelle` subset) spread across 679 classes, each label-attention query gets more signal per class than on CLINC150's 100-example intents, and at this data size it nearly closes the gap with Mean Pooling.

#### Stability

```{python}
#| label: fig-violin-naf
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of validation loss by architecture"

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in ARCHS_PRESENT:
    color = COLORS[arch]
    vals  = df[df["architecture"] == arch]["min_val_loss"].dropna()
    fig.add_trace(go.Violin(
        y=vals, name=arch,
        side="both",
        fillcolor=color, opacity=0.25,
        line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        box_visible=False, meanline_visible=False,
        points=False, showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
    ))
    fig.add_trace(go.Box(
        y=vals, name=arch,
        marker=dict(color=color, size=3, opacity=0.4),
        line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
        fillcolor="white", boxmean="sd", width=0.12,
        showlegend=False,
        hovertemplate="<b>" + arch + "</b><br>median=%{median:.4f}<br>Q1=%{q1:.4f}<br>Q3=%{q3:.4f}<extra></extra>",
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    template="simple_white",
    yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    yaxis=dict(gridcolor="#e8e8e8"),
    showlegend=False, height=430,
    violingap=0.4, boxgap=0.4,
)
fig.show()
```

FastText is also more stable, not just better on average: its results cluster tightly (std ≈0.014) while Label Attention spreads more than twice as wide (std ≈0.032), with a handful of runs tailing up past 0.60 — some hyperparameter combinations clearly suit label attention much worse than others.

:::

### Effect of vocabulary size and embedding dimension

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Vocabulary size

```{python}
#| label: fig-vocab-naf
#| fig-cap: "Effect of vocabulary size on validation loss"

vocab_vals = sorted(df["vocab_size"].dropna().unique())
emb_vals   = sorted(df["emb_dim"].dropna().unique())

df_vocab_mean = (
    df.groupby(["architecture", "vocab_size"], as_index=False)["min_val_loss"].mean()
    .sort_values("vocab_size")
)

vocab_offsets = {
    "FastText":                          -300,
    "FastText + Label Attention":        -100,
    "FATE (L=1)":                        +100,
    "FATE (L=1) + Label Attention":      +300,
}

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in ARCHS_PRESENT:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=True,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS[arch], size=8, opacity=1.0),
    ))
for arch, group in df.groupby("architecture"):
    offset = vocab_offsets.get(arch, 0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["vocab_size"] + offset, y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), size=5, opacity=0.15),
        hovertemplate="vocab=%{customdata:,}<br>val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        customdata=group["vocab_size"],
    ))
for arch, group in df_vocab_mean.groupby("architecture"):
    offset = vocab_offsets.get(arch, 0)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["vocab_size"] + offset, y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="lines+markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        line=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), width=2), marker=dict(size=6),
        hovertemplate="vocab=%{customdata:,}<br>mean val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        customdata=group["vocab_size"],
    ))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Vocabulary size", yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    xaxis=dict(tickvals=vocab_vals, ticktext=[f"{v:,}" for v in vocab_vals]),
    legend=dict(title=dict(text="Architecture<br><i style='font-size:11px;font-weight:normal'>line = mean</i>")),
    height=430, width=740, margin=dict(l=60, r=20),
)
fig.show()
```

Both architectures degrade slightly as vocabulary grows (FastText: 0.507→0.518, FastText + Label Attention: 0.519→0.545 from 2,000 to 20,000 tokens) — the same sparse-coverage effect as CLINC150, though milder here since NAF's larger corpus provides more gradient signal per token even at 20,000 vocab, and milder still than at the smaller `train_fraction` sweeps for the same reason.

### Training time

```{python}
#| label: fig-train-time-naf
#| fig-cap: "Validation loss vs. training time"

SYMBOLS = {"FastText": "circle", "FastText + Label Attention": "diamond"}

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in ARCHS_PRESENT:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=True,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS[arch], size=8, symbol=SYMBOLS.get(arch, "circle"), opacity=1.0),
    ))
for arch, group in df.groupby("architecture"):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["train_time_s"], y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        marker=dict(
            color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), size=7,
            symbol=SYMBOLS.get(arch, "circle"),
            opacity=0.65, line=dict(width=0.5, color="white"),
        ),
        hovertemplate="time=%{x:.0f}s<br>val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Training time (s)", yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    legend_title="Architecture", height=430,
    xaxis=dict(
        type="log",
        tickvals=[1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000],
        ticktext=["1k", "2k", "5k", "10k", "20k", "50k"],
    ),
)
fig.show()
```

Unlike CLINC150 — where label attention trained *faster* due to early stopping on a stalled loss — on NAF it trains markedly **slower** (mean ≈14,570s vs. ≈5,780s for FastText, an even wider gap than at the smaller `train_fraction` sweeps): with enough data to keep improving, label-attention runs keep going instead of stopping early, at real extra compute cost for a result that — at this data size — is now nearly on par.

### Interaction: embedding dimension × vocabulary size

```{python}
#| label: fig-heatmap-naf
#| fig-cap: "Mean validation loss by embedding dimension and vocabulary size"

import numpy as np
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

vmin = df.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size"])["min_val_loss"].mean().min()
vmax = df.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size"])["min_val_loss"].mean().max()

n_cols_hm = min(2, len(ARCHS_PRESENT))
n_rows_hm = (len(ARCHS_PRESENT) + n_cols_hm - 1) // n_cols_hm
fig = make_subplots(rows=n_rows_hm, cols=n_cols_hm, subplot_titles=ARCHS_PRESENT,
                    horizontal_spacing=0.08, vertical_spacing=0.28)

for idx, arch in enumerate(ARCHS_PRESENT):
    row, col = divmod(idx, n_cols_hm)
    pivot = (
        df[df["architecture"] == arch]
        .groupby(["emb_dim", "vocab_size"])["min_val_loss"].mean()
        .unstack("vocab_size")
        .reindex(index=emb_vals, columns=vocab_vals)
    )
    x_labels = [f"{v // 1000}k" for v in vocab_vals]
    y_labels = [str(v) for v in emb_vals]

    # go.Heatmap's textfont.color can't take a per-cell array, so contrast-aware
    # labels (white on dark cells, dark on light cells) are drawn as two masked
    # heatmap traces sharing one colorscale/zmin/zmax — each only "owns" the
    # cells matching its text color, NaN elsewhere so they tile into one heatmap.
    is_dark = (pivot.values - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) > 0.65
    for mask, text_color, show_scale in [(~is_dark, "#333333", idx == 0), (is_dark, "#ffffff", False)]:
        z_masked = np.where(mask, pivot.values, np.nan)
        fig.add_trace(go.Heatmap(
            z=z_masked,
            x=x_labels,
            y=y_labels,
            colorscale="Viridis_r",
            zmin=vmin, zmax=vmax,
            text=[[f"{v:.3f}" if not np.isnan(v) else "" for v in row_] for row_ in z_masked],
            texttemplate="%{text}",
            textfont=dict(color=text_color),
            showscale=show_scale,
            colorbar=dict(title="Mean val loss", orientation="h", x=0.5, xanchor="center",
                          y=-0.38, yanchor="top", len=0.5, thickness=18, title_side="bottom") if show_scale else None,
            hovertemplate="vocab=%{x}<br>emb_dim=%{y}<br>val_loss=%{z:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        ), row=row + 1, col=col + 1)
    fig.update_yaxes(
        title_text="Embedding dim" if col == 0 else "",
        range=[-0.5, len(y_labels) - 0.5], row=row + 1, col=col + 1,
    )
    fig.update_xaxes(
        title_text="Vocabulary size", title_font=dict(size=12), tickangle=0,
        range=[-0.5, len(x_labels) - 0.5], row=row + 1, col=col + 1,
    )
    # force square cells — scaleanchor ties this subplot's y-axis pixel scale to its own x-axis
    xaxis_id = "x" if idx == 0 else f"x{idx + 1}"
    fig.update_yaxes(scaleanchor=xaxis_id, scaleratio=1, constrain="domain", row=row + 1, col=col + 1)
    fig.update_xaxes(constrain="domain", row=row + 1, col=col + 1)

for ann in fig.layout.annotations:
    ann.update(font=dict(size=12))
fig.update_layout(height=500, width=790, margin=dict(l=50, r=20, t=40, b=130))
fig.show()
```

The two knobs don't interact much for FastText — the best cell (emb_dim=128, vocab=2,000, 0.494) and worst (emb_dim=512, vocab=20,000, 0.529) are both corner cases, and the grid is fairly flat in between. Label Attention is more sensitive to vocabulary size, and it compounds with embedding dimension: at emb_dim=64, growing the vocab from 2,000 to 20,000 alone pushes the loss from 0.518 to 0.559 — the single worst cell in the whole grid, and a much bigger swing than the same vocab change produces at emb_dim=128 (0.515→0.541).

## Prediction analysis

This section examines what the models actually predict, using the best (`train_fraction=0.26`) run of each architecture available so far. Only `FastText` and `FastText + Label Attention` have predictions today — `FATE (L=1)` will be added once its sweep on `train_fraction=0.26` completes. With 679 sub-class targets, a full per-class confusion matrix or example view (as used for Amazon's 5 classes and CLINC150's 150) would be unreadable — figures below are adapted to this scale: errors are aggregated to the 21 **sections** (the coarsest NAF level) wherever a per-class view would be unreadable, and examples show the actual sub-class code and its official label rather than a bare class index.

```{python}
#| label: load-predictions-naf

import json
import urllib.request
import numpy as np
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import HTML

PRED_BUCKET = "https://minio.lab.sspcloud.fr/projet-text-classif/predictions/naf"
ARCH_FILES  = {
    "FastText":                   "fasttext.npz",
    "FastText + Label Attention": "fasttext_labatt.npz",
}

PREDS_DIR = Path("results/naf/preds")
PREDS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

preds_by_arch = {}   # arch -> {"y_test": ..., "y_pred": ..., "X_test": ...}

for arch, fname in ARCH_FILES.items():
    cache = PREDS_DIR / fname
    try:
        if not cache.exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{PRED_BUCKET}/{fname}", cache)
        d = np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True)
        preds_by_arch[arch] = {
            "y_test": d["y_test"].astype(int),
            "y_pred": d["y_pred"].astype(int),
            "X_test": d["X_test"],
        }
    except Exception:
        pass

ARCHS_AVAIL = list(preds_by_arch.keys())

# Reconstructs the class index -> NAF sub-class code mapping produced by the
# sklearn LabelEncoder in src/train.py (see assets/naf_labels.json for how it was built).
with open("assets/naf_labels.json") as f:
    NAF_LABEL_MAP = json.load(f)  # {"0": "0111Y", ...}

with open("assets/naf2025_structure.json") as f:
    _naf_struct = json.load(f)

DIVISION_TO_SECTION = {
    div: s["id"] for s in _naf_struct["sections"] for div in s["divisions"]
}
SECTION_LABEL = {s["id"]: s["label"] for s in _naf_struct["sections"]}
SECTION_ORDER = [s["id"] for s in _naf_struct["sections"]]
SOUSCLASSE_LABEL = _naf_struct["sousclasses"]  # keyed like "01.11Y"

def class_code(idx: int) -> str:
    return NAF_LABEL_MAP.get(str(idx), "?")

def code_section(code: str) -> str:
    return DIVISION_TO_SECTION.get(code[:2], "?")

def code_division(code: str) -> str:
    return code[:2]

def code_groupe(code: str) -> str:
    return code[:2] + "." + code[2:3]

def code_classe(code: str) -> str:
    return code[:2] + "." + code[2:4]

def code_label(code: str) -> str:
    dotted = code[:2] + "." + code[2:]
    return SOUSCLASSE_LABEL.get(dotted, code)

SECTION_COLOR = {s["id"]: s["color"] for s in _naf_struct["sections"]}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Accuracy vs. class support

With 679 sub-classes drawn from a corpus that is nowhere near uniform across them, a natural question is: **do errors concentrate in the sub-classes that simply have the fewest training examples?** Each point below is one sub-class; x is how many test examples it has (log scale), y is the model's accuracy restricted to that sub-class.

```{python}
#| label: fig-support-acc-naf
#| fig-cap: "Per-sub-class accuracy vs. number of test examples for that sub-class (log x-axis)"

COLORS = {"FastText": "#2196F3", "FastText + Label Attention": "#00BCD4"}

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL:
    d = preds_by_arch[arch]
    y_test_a, y_pred_a = d["y_test"], d["y_pred"]
    classes_present = np.unique(y_test_a)
    support = np.array([(y_test_a == c).sum() for c in classes_present])
    accuracy = np.array([
        (y_pred_a[y_test_a == c] == c).mean() for c in classes_present
    ])
    hover_codes = [class_code(c) for c in classes_present]
    hover_labels = [code_label(c) for c in hover_codes]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=support, y=accuracy * 100, mode="markers", name=arch,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), size=6, opacity=0.55,
                    line=dict(width=0.5, color="white")),
        customdata=np.stack([hover_codes, hover_labels], axis=1),
        hovertemplate="<b>%{customdata[0]} — %{customdata[1]}</b><br>"
                      "test support=%{x}<br>accuracy=%{y:.1f}%<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

TICK_VALS = [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000]
TICK_TEXT = ["1", "2", "5", "10", "20", "50", "100", "200", "500", "1k", "2k", "5k", "10k"]

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Test-set support for this sub-class (log scale)",
    yaxis_title="Accuracy on this sub-class (%)",
    xaxis=dict(type="log", tickvals=TICK_VALS, ticktext=TICK_TEXT),
    yaxis=dict(range=[-2, 102]),
    legend_title="Architecture", height=450,
)
fig.show()
```

The funnel shape confirms the hypothesis: below roughly 20 test examples, accuracy swings anywhere from 0% to 100%, but past a few hundred examples it tightens firmly into the 80–100% band. Errors concentrate in the least-represented sub-classes, and the model gets both more accurate and more stable once a sub-class clears a few hundred examples.

### Hierarchical accuracy

The 679-way exact-match accuracy used everywhere else is the strictest possible reading of a wrong prediction — a sub-class miss can still land in the right section, division, group, or class. The two views below unpack this using the NAF hierarchy.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hierarchy-cascade-naf
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy by required hierarchy level"

LEVELS = [
    ("Section",   code_section),
    ("Division",  code_division),
    ("Group",     code_groupe),
    ("Class",     code_classe),
    ("Sub-class", lambda c: c),
]

cascade_err = {}  # arch -> [error rate at each LEVELS entry, coarse to fine]
for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL:
    d = preds_by_arch[arch]
    true_codes = [class_code(c) for c in d["y_test"]]
    pred_codes = [class_code(c) for c in d["y_pred"]]
    cascade_err[arch] = [
        100 - np.mean([fn(t) == fn(p) for t, p in zip(true_codes, pred_codes)]) * 100
        for _, fn in LEVELS
    ]

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[lvl for lvl, _ in LEVELS], y=cascade_err[arch], mode="lines+markers", name=arch,
        line=dict(color=COLORS.get(arch, "grey"), width=2.5), marker=dict(size=10),
        hovertemplate="%{x}<br>error rate=%{y:.1f}%<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    template="simple_white",
    xaxis_title="Required level of agreement", yaxis_title="Error rate (%)",
    yaxis=dict(rangemode="tozero"),
    legend_title="Architecture", height=430,
)
fig.show()
```

As expected, the error rate stays low and climbs only gradually as the required match gets stricter: ≈7% wrong at section level, rising to ≈14–15% wrong requiring the exact sub-class — most predictions are precise enough that relaxing the granularity doesn't recover much extra accuracy. Plotting the error rate instead of the accuracy also means the y-axis can start at a meaningful zero without truncating anything, so the small-but-real climb is actually visible instead of being flattened against a 0–100% accuracy scale.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hierarchy-errors-naf
#| fig-cap: "Among wrong predictions, the coarsest NAF level at which they still land correctly"

ERROR_BUCKETS = ["Class", "Group", "Division", "Section", "No match"]
BUCKET_COLORS = {
    "Class":      "#66BB6A",
    "Group":      "#FFCA28",
    "Division":   "#FB8C00",
    "Section":    "#E53935",
    "No match":   "#7B0000",
}


def _finest_match(true_code: str, pred_code: str) -> str:
    for name, fn in reversed(LEVELS):
        if fn(true_code) == fn(pred_code):
            return name
    return "No match"


error_shares = {}  # arch -> {bucket: pct of errors}
overall_acc = {}  # arch -> exact-match accuracy, for the x-axis subtitle
for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL:
    d = preds_by_arch[arch]
    true_codes = [class_code(c) for c in d["y_test"]]
    pred_codes = [class_code(c) for c in d["y_pred"]]
    buckets = [_finest_match(t, p) for t, p in zip(true_codes, pred_codes)]
    overall_acc[arch] = (pd.Series(buckets) == "Sub-class").mean() * 100
    errors = [b for b in buckets if b != "Sub-class"]
    counts = pd.Series(errors).value_counts()
    error_shares[arch] = {b: counts.get(b, 0) / len(errors) * 100 for b in ERROR_BUCKETS}

x_labels = [
    f"{arch}<br><i>({100 - overall_acc[arch]:.1f}% of test set is wrong)</i>"
    for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL
]

fig = go.Figure()
for bucket in ERROR_BUCKETS:
    vals = [error_shares[arch][bucket] for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL]
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=x_labels, y=vals, name=bucket,
        marker=dict(color=BUCKET_COLORS[bucket]),
        text=[f"{v:.1f}%" for v in vals],
        textposition="inside", insidetextfont=dict(color="white", size=11),
        hovertemplate="%{x}<br>" + bucket + ": %{y:.1f}% of errors<extra></extra>",
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    template="simple_white", barmode="stack",
    xaxis_title=None, yaxis_title="Share of wrong predictions (%)",
    yaxis=dict(range=[0, 100]),
    legend_title="Coarsest level where<br>the miss still lands right", height=480,
)
fig.show()
```

Zooming into the wrong predictions only, that small gap hides a less reassuring story: only ≈8% of errors stay within the correct **class**, while the single largest bucket by far — **≈48–50%** — is "No match", missing even the broad section. The model's overall accuracy looks stable across granularity, but that's an average masking two very different failure modes: most predictions are exactly right, and most of the rest are wildly wrong.

### Top section confusions

The accuracy-vs-support and hierarchical-accuracy views above show that errors happen and roughly how far off they land, but not *which* sections bleed into which. With 21 sections, a full flow diagram between all of them turns into an unreadable tangle — this view instead ranks the single biggest **misclassification flows** (correct predictions excluded): which true section, predicted as which other section, accounts for the most errors.

```{python}
#| label: fig-topflows-naf
#| fig-cap: "Top misclassification flows between NAF sections (true section → predicted section)"

N_FLOWS = 15


def _top_flows(arch):
    d = preds_by_arch[arch]
    true_sec = [code_section(class_code(y)) for y in d["y_test"]]
    pred_sec = [code_section(class_code(y)) for y in d["y_pred"]]
    flow_counts = defaultdict(int)
    for t, p in zip(true_sec, pred_sec):
        if t != p:
            flow_counts[(t, p)] += 1
    top = sorted(flow_counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)[:N_FLOWS]
    return top[::-1]  # reversed: largest ends up at the top of the horizontal bar


n_archs = len(ARCHS_AVAIL)
fig = go.Figure()

for i, arch in enumerate(ARCHS_AVAIL):
    top = _top_flows(arch)
    labels = [f"{t} → {p}" for (t, p), _ in top]
    counts = [cnt for _, cnt in top]
    colors = [SECTION_COLOR.get(t, "#888888") for (t, p), _ in top]
    hover = [f"{SECTION_LABEL.get(t, t)} → {SECTION_LABEL.get(p, p)}" for (t, p), _ in top]
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=counts, y=labels, orientation="h",
        marker=dict(color=colors),
        customdata=hover,
        text=[str(c) for c in counts], textposition="outside",
        hovertemplate="<b>%{customdata}</b><br>%{x} misclassifications<extra></extra>",
        visible=(i == 0),
    ))

buttons = [dict(
    label=arch, method="update",
    args=[{"visible": [j == i for j in range(n_archs)]}],
) for i, arch in enumerate(ARCHS_AVAIL)]

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of misclassifications (true → predicted section)",
    yaxis_title=None,
    height=550, margin=dict(l=10, r=40, t=60, b=40),
    updatemenus=[dict(
        type="dropdown", buttons=buttons,
        x=0.5, xanchor="center", y=1.08, yanchor="top",
        showactive=True, bgcolor="#f0f0f0", bordercolor="#ccc",
        font=dict(size=12),
    )],
)
fig.show()
```

## Explainability

This section turns the spotlight on *why* the models predict what they predict, not just *how often* they're right. The analysis is built around a focused comparison: **FastText** against **FastText + Label Attention** (identical architecture and hyperparameters, mean pooling vs. label attention as the sole difference). Both models are probed with an identical battery of analyses on the *same* 200 sampled test descriptions, so every figure below is a direct, paired comparison rather than two separate reports glued together.

NAF differs from Amazon (5 classes) and CLINC150 (150 classes) in one important way: **679 sub-classes**. Several views used on those pages (a full class × class correlation matrix, one line per class, etc.) would simply be unreadable at this scale, so the figures below either aggregate up to the 21 NAF **sections** (the same coarsest level used in Prediction analysis above) or select a representative subset of sub-classes. There is also no self-attention view here: Amazon and CLINC150 are built on a transformer backbone, but the NAF models compared here are **FastText** and **FastText + Label Attention** — bag-of-embeddings architectures with no self-attention layer, so that instrument doesn't apply.

Four complementary instruments are used throughout:

- **Layer Integrated Gradients (Captum)**: a gradient-based, post-hoc attribution method that assigns every input word a *signed* score for every class: positive = pushes the prediction toward that class, negative = pushes away. It only needs a forward+backward pass through the model, so it can be computed identically for both architectures.
- **Label-attention weights**: for the Label Attention model only: the *raw cross-attention weights* between each class query and the description's tokens. An explanation that's *built into* the architecture, rather than reconstructed after the fact.
- **Class direction vectors**: two matrices, one per model, each with one vector per sub-class: the label-attention queries (`label_embeds`, 679×64) from the Label Attention model, and the weight matrix of the linear classification head (`linear_weight`, 679×512) from FastText. `linear_weight` rows are dotted directly with the pooled embedding to produce a logit; `label_embeds` rows are attention queries used earlier in the pipeline, with no direct competitive pressure — the two live at very different points in the network.
- **A faithfulness (word-deletion) stress test**: attribution scores are only useful if they reflect what the model *actually* relies on, so we test this directly: delete the highest-scoring words and watch the predicted probability collapse (or not).

```{python}
#| label: load-explain-artifacts-naf

import urllib.request

EXPLAIN_BUCKET_NAF  = "https://minio.lab.sspcloud.fr/projet-text-classif/explanations/naf"
_ARTIFACT_NAMES_NAF = ["captum.npz", "label_attn.npz", "class_vectors.npz", "faithfulness.npz"]
_NOT_APPLICABLE_NAF = {("pooling", "label_attn.npz")}  # mean pooling has no label attention mechanism

def _load_artifact_naf(method: str, name: str):
    """Fetch (and cache) one NAF explainability artifact; None if unavailable."""
    if (method, name) in _NOT_APPLICABLE_NAF:
        return None
    cache_dir = Path("results/naf/explain") / method
    cache_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    cache = cache_dir / name
    try:
        if not cache.exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{EXPLAIN_BUCKET_NAF}/{method}/{name}", cache)
        return np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True)
    except Exception:
        return None

cap_la, lat_la, cv_la, fai_la = (_load_artifact_naf("labatt",  n) for n in _ARTIFACT_NAMES_NAF)
cap_pl, lat_pl, cv_pl, fai_pl = (_load_artifact_naf("pooling", n) for n in _ARTIFACT_NAMES_NAF)

HAS_LA   = cap_la is not None
HAS_PL   = cap_pl is not None
HAS_BOTH = HAS_LA and HAS_PL

if not HAS_LA:
    print("Explainability artifacts not yet available — re-run src/explain.py")
else:
    N_CLS = cap_la["word_attn"][0].shape[0]

    # Short NAF codes for axis/tick labels, full official labels for prose — the
    # official label ("Culture de céréales, à l'exception du riz...") is far too
    # long to use as a tick label at 679-class scale.
    CLASS_CODE  = [class_code(i) for i in range(N_CLS)]
    CLASS_LABEL = [code_label(c) for c in CLASS_CODE]
    CLASS_SEC   = [code_section(c) for c in CLASS_CODE]
    SECTION_COLOR = {s["id"]: s["color"] for s in _naf_struct["sections"]}
    PALETTE = [SECTION_COLOR.get(sec, "#888888") for sec in CLASS_SEC]

    MODEL_LABELS = {"labatt": "FastText + Label Attention", "pooling": "FastText"}
    CAPTUM     = {"labatt": cap_la, "pooling": cap_pl}
    LABEL_ATTN = {"labatt": lat_la, "pooling": lat_pl}
    CLASS_VECS = {"labatt": cv_la,  "pooling": cv_pl}
    FAITHFUL   = {"labatt": fai_la, "pooling": fai_pl}
    MODEL_KEYS = [k for k in ("labatt", "pooling") if CAPTUM[k] is not None]

    def _class_sorted(cap, i: int) -> np.ndarray:
        """Reorder word_attn[i]'s rows from confidence rank back to actual class index."""
        inv = np.argsort(cap["class_order"][i])
        return cap["word_attn"][i][inv]
```

### Word attributions

The fastest way to *trust* or distrust an explanation is to look at it on a real description. The figure below renders a handful of test descriptions as **highlighted text**: each word's background is shaded in proportion to its Captum attribution score. **Green = pushes toward the selected sub-class, red = pushes away from it**, with colour intensity proportional to `|score| / max|score|` within that description. When a model predicts incorrectly, you can toggle between **predicted** and **true** class to compare what the model *thought* it was reading versus what it should have read.

The selection covers four informative cases: descriptions where the two architectures **disagree** on the predicted sub-class; a couple where they **agree and are correct**; cases where **both are wrong**; and cases where **FastText is correct but FastText + Label Attention is not**.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-highlight-naf
#| fig-cap: "Highlighted-text view of Captum attributions. When pred ≠ true, toggle between predicted and true class."
import json
from IPython.display import HTML, display

if not HAS_LA:
    out = HTML("<p>Artifacts not yet available.</p>")
else:
    y_true_la = cap_la["y_true"].astype(int)
    y_pred_la = cap_la["y_pred"].astype(int)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

    def _cls_display(idx: int) -> str:
        return f"{CLASS_CODE[idx]} — {CLASS_LABEL[idx]}"

    picks: list = []
    if HAS_BOTH:
        y_pred_pl = cap_pl["y_pred"].astype(int)
        disagree  = np.where(y_pred_la != y_pred_pl)[0]
        rng.shuffle(disagree)
        picks += disagree[:3].tolist()
        agree_ok = np.where((y_pred_la == y_pred_pl) & (y_pred_la == y_true_la))[0]
        rng.shuffle(agree_ok)
        picks += [int(i) for i in agree_ok if i not in picks][:2]
        both_wrong = np.where((y_pred_la != y_true_la) & (y_pred_pl != y_true_la))[0]
        rng.shuffle(both_wrong)
        picks += [int(i) for i in both_wrong if i not in picks][:2]
        pl_right_la_wrong = np.where((y_pred_pl == y_true_la) & (y_pred_la != y_true_la))[0]
        rng.shuffle(pl_right_la_wrong)
        picks += [int(i) for i in pl_right_la_wrong if i not in picks][:2]
    else:
        ok = np.where(y_pred_la == y_true_la)[0]
        rng.shuffle(ok)
        picks = ok[:5].tolist()

    examples_explain = []
    for i in picks:
        i = int(i)
        y_true_i = int(cap_la["y_true"][i])
        words = [str(w) for w in list(cap_la["words"][i])[:40]]
        entry = {
            "y_true": y_true_i,
            "text":   str(cap_la["texts"][i])[:200],
            "models": [],
        }
        for key in MODEL_KEYS:
            cap  = CAPTUM[key]
            pred = int(cap["y_pred"][i])
            mat  = _class_sorted(cap, i)
            nw   = len(words)
            entry["models"].append({
                "name":        MODEL_LABELS[key],
                "pred":        pred,
                "words":       words,
                "pred_scores": mat[pred][:nw].tolist(),
                "true_scores": mat[y_true_i][:nw].tolist() if pred != y_true_i else None,
            })
        examples_explain.append(entry)

    def _spans_html(words, scores):
        amax = max((abs(s) for s in scores), default=1) or 1
        parts = []
        for j, w in enumerate(words):
            s = scores[j] if j < len(scores) else 0
            t = abs(s) / amax
            rgb = "57,255,20" if s >= 0 else "255,30,30"
            alpha = round(0.10 + 0.65 * t, 2)
            parts.append(
                f'<span style="background-color:rgba({rgb},{alpha});'
                f'padding:1px 3px;margin:0 1px;line-height:2.3;">{w}</span>'
            )
        return " ".join(parts)

    cards_html = []
    for ex in examples_explain:
        y_true = ex["y_true"]
        meta = (
            f'<div style="font-size:13px;color:#444;margin-bottom:10px;">'
            f'<b>true sub-class:</b> <span style="font-weight:700;">{_cls_display(y_true)}</span>'
            f' &mdash; <i>&ldquo;{ex["text"]}&rdquo;</i></div>'
        )
        models_html = ""
        for m in ex["models"]:
            ok  = m["pred"] == y_true
            bc  = "#2E7D32" if ok else "#B71C1C"
            mark = "✓ correct" if ok else "✗ incorrect"
            models_html += (
                f'<div style="margin:6px 0 12px 0;">'
                f'<div style="font-size:12.5px;color:#555;margin-bottom:4px;">'
                f'<b>{m["name"]}</b> → predicts '
                f'<span style="color:#222;font-weight:700;">{_cls_display(m["pred"])}</span> '
                f'<span style="color:{bc};font-size:11px;">({mark})</span>'
                f'</div>'
            )
            models_html += (
                f'<div style="font-size:11px;color:#777;margin-bottom:2px;">predicted class</div>'
                f'<div style="line-height:2.5;">{_spans_html(m["words"], m["pred_scores"])}</div>'
            )
            if m["true_scores"] is not None:
                models_html += (
                    f'<div style="font-size:11px;color:#777;margin:6px 0 2px 0;">true class</div>'
                    f'<div style="line-height:2.5;">{_spans_html(m["words"], m["true_scores"])}</div>'
                )
            models_html += "</div>"
        cards_html.append(
            f'<div style="border:1px solid #e2e2e2;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;'
            f'background:#fcfcfc;">{meta}{models_html}</div>'
        )

    nav_id = "hl-nav-naf"
    n_cards = len(cards_html)
```

### Corpus-level word importance

Zooming out from individual descriptions: which words does each architecture rely on *in general* for each **section**? Rather than displaying 679 per-class charts, we aggregate the Captum scores across all sub-classes within each of the 21 NAF sections, keeping only words seen at least 3 times. This gives a compact view of the vocabulary each section relies on — and whether the two architectures agree on what matters.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-corpus-naf
#| fig-cap: "Top-12 most positively-attributed words per section (mean signed Captum IG score averaged across all sub-classes in the section, words seen ≥ 3 times)."

TOP_K = 12

def _corpus_acc_naf(cap) -> list:
    acc = [defaultdict(list) for _ in range(N_CLS)]
    for i, wds in enumerate(cap["words"]):
        mat = _class_sorted(cap, i)
        for c in range(N_CLS):
            for j, w in enumerate(list(wds)):
                if j < mat.shape[1]:
                    acc[c][w.lower()].append(float(mat[c, j]))
    return acc

def _section_top(accs_per_cls, k=TOP_K, min_count=3):
    combined = defaultdict(list)
    for a in accs_per_cls:
        for w, v in a.items():
            combined[w].extend(v)
    means = {w: float(np.mean(v)) for w, v in combined.items() if len(v) >= min_count}
    return sorted(means.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:k]

if not HAS_LA:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    accs_naf = {k: _corpus_acc_naf(CAPTUM[k]) for k in MODEL_KEYS}

    section_to_cls = defaultdict(list)
    for i in range(N_CLS):
        section_to_cls[CLASS_SEC[i]].append(i)

    ROWS, COLS = 3, 7
    fig_corp_naf = make_subplots(
        rows=ROWS, cols=COLS,
        subplot_titles=SECTION_ORDER,
        horizontal_spacing=0.045,
        vertical_spacing=0.10,
    )

    for ki, key in enumerate(MODEL_KEYS):
        for si, sec in enumerate(SECTION_ORDER):
            row = si // COLS + 1
            col = si % COLS + 1
            top    = _section_top([accs_naf[key][c] for c in section_to_cls[sec]])[::-1]
            ws     = [w for w, _ in top]
            ss     = [s for _, s in top]
            colors = [SECTION_COLOR[sec] if s >= 0 else "#ef5350" for s in ss]
            fig_corp_naf.add_trace(go.Bar(
                x=ss, y=ws, orientation="h",
                marker=dict(color=colors, line=dict(width=0)),
                width=0.55, opacity=0.88, showlegend=False,
                visible=(ki == 0),
                hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>Mean IG: %{x:.4f}<extra></extra>",
            ), row=row, col=col)

    for si, sec in enumerate(SECTION_ORDER):
        row, col = si // COLS + 1, si % COLS + 1
        fig_corp_naf.update_xaxes(
            showgrid=True, gridcolor="#f0f0f0", zeroline=True, zerolinecolor="#aaa",
            tickfont=dict(size=8), row=row, col=col,
        )
        fig_corp_naf.update_yaxes(tickfont=dict(size=8), showgrid=False, row=row, col=col)

    for i, ann in enumerate(fig_corp_naf.layout.annotations):
        if i < len(SECTION_ORDER):
            ann.font.size = 12
            ann.font.color = SECTION_COLOR[SECTION_ORDER[i]]

    layout_extra = {}
    if HAS_BOTH:
        n_tr = len(SECTION_ORDER)
        vis  = {key: [j // n_tr == ki for j in range(n_tr * len(MODEL_KEYS))]
                for ki, key in enumerate(MODEL_KEYS)}
        layout_extra = dict(updatemenus=[dict(
            type="buttons", direction="right", active=0,
            buttons=[dict(label=MODEL_LABELS[k], method="restyle",
                          args=[{"visible": vis[k]}]) for k in MODEL_KEYS],
            x=0.5, xanchor="center", y=1.04, yanchor="bottom",
            showactive=True, bgcolor="#f5f5f5", bordercolor="#ddd", borderwidth=1,
            font=dict(size=12, color="#222"), pad=dict(l=8, r=8, t=4, b=4),
        )])

    fig_corp_naf.update_layout(
        height=1000,
        margin=dict(t=100 if HAS_BOTH else 60, b=30, l=20, r=20),
        paper_bgcolor="white", plot_bgcolor="white",
        **layout_extra,
    )
    fig_corp_naf.show()
```

### Distinctiveness of per-class explanations

A raw 679×679 correlation matrix is unreadable. A more informative approach is to *select* the most interesting sub-classes according to a precise criterion. Two views are shown below, each answering a different question about the attribution profiles. Use the buttons to switch between the two models. Axis labels are the short NAF sub-class codes (hover for the full official label).

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-class-correlation-shared-naf
#| include: false

def _class_corpus_matrix_naf(acc, min_count=3):
    vocab = sorted({w for c in acc for w, v in c.items() if len(v) >= min_count})
    mat = np.zeros((N_CLS, len(vocab)))
    for c in range(N_CLS):
        for j, w in enumerate(vocab):
            v = acc[c].get(w)
            if v and len(v) >= min_count:
                mat[c, j] = float(np.mean(v))
    return mat, vocab

_cls_mats_naf  = {}
_cls_corrs_naf = {}
if HAS_LA:
    for key in MODEL_KEYS:
        m, _v = _class_corpus_matrix_naf(accs_naf[key])
        _cls_mats_naf[key]  = m
        _cls_corrs_naf[key] = np.corrcoef(m)
```

#### Most-confused sub-classes

We select the **20 sub-classes with the highest error rate** (FastText + Label Attention model) and display the 20×20 sub-matrix of their word-attribution profiles. If the model confuses sub-classes A and B, their attribution profiles should look similar (high positive correlation). Hot off-diagonal cells reveal sub-class pairs that are simultaneously hard to classify *and* hard to distinguish in attribution space.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-class-correlation-confused-naf
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlation between word-attribution profiles for the 20 most-confused sub-classes. High off-diagonal values suggest the model assigns similar lexical signatures to different sub-classes."

if not HAS_LA:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    ref_key = MODEL_KEYS[0]
    y_true_ref = CAPTUM[ref_key]["y_true"].astype(int)
    y_pred_ref = CAPTUM[ref_key]["y_pred"].astype(int)
    error_rates = np.array([
        1.0 - (y_pred_ref[y_true_ref == c] == c).mean()
        if (y_true_ref == c).sum() > 0 else 0.0
        for c in range(N_CLS)
    ])
    top_confused_naf = sorted(np.argsort(error_rates)[::-1][:_N_SEL_NAF].tolist())
    sel_codes_a  = [CLASS_CODE[c] for c in top_confused_naf]
    sel_hover_a  = [f"{CLASS_CODE[c]} — {CLASS_LABEL[c]}" for c in top_confused_naf]
    _full_corr_fig_naf(top_confused_naf, sel_codes_a, sel_hover_a).show()
```

#### Most similar sub-class pairs

We identify the **20 sub-classes involved in the highest-correlation pairs** (highest off-diagonal r in the FastText + Label Attention matrix). These are sub-classes for which the model produces nearly identical explanations despite different NAF codes — potential blind spots. The sub-matrix reveals their similarity structure.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-class-correlation-similar-naf
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlation between word-attribution profiles for the 20 sub-classes involved in the most similar pairs (highest off-diagonal r). These sub-classes share nearly identical lexical signatures despite being formally distinct."

if not HAS_LA:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    corr_ref = _cls_corrs_naf[MODEL_KEYS[0]].copy()
    np.fill_diagonal(corr_ref, -np.inf)
    flat_idx = np.argsort(corr_ref.ravel())[::-1]
    seen: set = set()
    for idx in flat_idx:
        i, j = divmod(int(idx), N_CLS)
        seen.add(i); seen.add(j)
        if len(seen) >= _N_SEL_NAF:
            break
    top_similar_naf = sorted(list(seen)[:_N_SEL_NAF])
    sel_codes_c = [CLASS_CODE[c] for c in top_similar_naf]
    sel_hover_c = [f"{CLASS_CODE[c]} — {CLASS_LABEL[c]}" for c in top_similar_naf]
    _full_corr_fig_naf(top_similar_naf, sel_codes_c, sel_hover_c).show()
```

### Class representations: label queries vs. linear-head directions

At the very last step, both architectures reduce a description to a decision by comparing some representation of the description against **one reference vector per sub-class**:

- FastText + Label Attention learns 679 **query embeddings** (`label_embeds`) that drive the cross-attention: they are the model's notion of "what a `6210Y` description sounds like", "what a `4791A` description sounds like", etc.
- FastText learns a plain **linear classification head**; each of its 679 weight rows (`linear_weight`) plays the same role: the direction in embedding space onto which the pooled description vector is projected for that sub-class.

The two matrices don't even share a dimension (679×64 vs. 679×512): the same caveats as for Amazon and CLINC150 apply — `linear_weight` rows live in a *competitive* space (each row is dotted directly with the pooled embedding to produce a logit, so rows must spread out), whereas `label_embeds` rows are *attention queries* whose geometry has no direct competitive pressure and is several non-linear steps removed from the final decision.

**(a) Cosine similarity matrix**: reusing the same 20 most-confused sub-classes selected above, how aligned are their class vectors with one another, within each model? Visible block structure would reveal clusters of sub-classes whose internal representations are close.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-class-cosine-naf
#| fig-cap: "Cosine similarity between the class vectors of the 20 most-confused sub-classes, per model."

def _cosine_sim_naf(vecs: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    n = vecs / (np.linalg.norm(vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-12)
    return n @ n.T

def _pca_2d_naf(vecs: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    centered = vecs - vecs.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    _, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd(centered, full_matrices=False)
    return centered @ Vt[:2].T

HAS_CV_NAF = HAS_LA and all(CLASS_VECS.get(k) is not None for k in MODEL_KEYS)

if not HAS_CV_NAF:
    print("Class-vector artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    titles_naf = [f"{MODEL_LABELS[k]}<br><sub>({str(CLASS_VECS[k]['kind'])})</sub>" for k in MODEL_KEYS]
    fig_cos_naf = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=len(MODEL_KEYS), subplot_titles=titles_naf)
    for ci, key in enumerate(MODEL_KEYS):
        vecs = CLASS_VECS[key]["class_vectors"][top_confused_naf]
        sim  = _cosine_sim_naf(vecs)
        fig_cos_naf.add_trace(go.Heatmap(
            z=sim, x=sel_codes_a, y=sel_codes_a, zmin=-1, zmax=1, colorscale="RdBu_r",
            showscale=(ci == len(MODEL_KEYS) - 1), colorbar=dict(title="cos"),
            hovertemplate="x=%{x}<br>y=%{y}<br>cos=%{z:.3f}<extra></extra>",
        ), row=1, col=ci + 1)
    fig_cos_naf.update_yaxes(autorange="reversed")
    fig_cos_naf.update_xaxes(tickfont=dict(size=9), tickangle=-90)
    fig_cos_naf.update_yaxes(tickfont=dict(size=9))
    fig_cos_naf.update_layout(
        height=560, paper_bgcolor="white", plot_bgcolor="white",
        margin=dict(t=60, b=80, l=80, r=10),
    )
    fig_cos_naf.show()
```

**(b) 2D PCA projection**: we project all 679 class vectors onto their first two principal components, coloured by NAF **section**. A tight, undifferentiated cloud suggests the model relies primarily on magnitude rather than direction; visible clusters — especially ones that align with section colour — would confirm that the model has organised the sub-class space geometrically along lines that echo the official NAF hierarchy, even though the model is never given section labels during training. With 679 points, individual text labels would be unreadable, so hover over a point to see its code and official label.

```{python}
            showlegend=False,

        ), row=1, col=ci + 1)

    fig_pca_naf.update_yaxes(title_text="PC2", col=1)
```

### Inside label attention: does the mechanism agree with post-hoc explanations?

Label Attention's built-in explanation — cross-attention weights, one query per sub-class over the description — can be compared directly against the gradient-based Captum scores. If the two agree, it is reassuring triangulation: the model's internal routing mechanism and the post-hoc attribution converge on the same words. If they disagree, the label-attention weights are not a faithful account of what drives the prediction.

**(a) Side-by-side view.** Unlike the Amazon/CLINC150 pages, this doesn't offer a full class dropdown — with 679 sub-classes a selector would be unusable — so, as in the word-attributions figure above, you can toggle between the **predicted** and **true** class when they differ.

```{python}
         + '<select class="hl2-toggle" onchange="hl2ToggleNaf(' + i + ',this.value)">'
         + '<option value="pred"' + (wantTrue ? '' : ' selected') + '>predicted class</option>'
         + '<option value="true"' + (wantTrue ? ' selected' : '') + '>true class</option>'
         + '</select></div>';
    }}
    const capScores = wantTrue ? e.captum_true : e.captum_pred;
    const latScores = wantTrue ? e.labatt_true : e.labatt_pred;
    h += '<div class="hl2-row">'
       + '<div class="hl2-rlbl"><b>Captum IG</b> <span style="font-size:11px;color:#888;">(green = for / red = against, gradient-based)</span></div>'
       + '<div class="hl2-words">' + spansSigned(e.words, capScores) + '</div>'
       + '</div>';
    h += '<div class="hl2-row">'
       + '<div class="hl2-rlbl"><b>Label Attention</b> <span style="font-size:11px;color:#888;">(blue = attention received, architecture-native)</span></div>'
       + '<div class="hl2-words">' + spansUnsigned(e.words, latScores) + '</div>'
       + '</div>';
    document.getElementById('hl2-naf-rows').innerHTML = h;
  }}

  window.hl2ToggleNaf = function(exIdx, val) {{
    selTrue[exIdx] = (val === 'true');
    render(cur);
  }};
  window.hl2NavNaf = function(d) {{ cur = (cur + d + EX.length) % EX.length; render(cur); }};
  render(0);
}})();
</script>
"""
        display(HTML(hl2_html))
```

**(b) Quantitative agreement: correlation distributions.** For each description, we compute the **Pearson correlation** between the label-attention weights and the absolute Captum scores at word level, *for the predicted class only* (with 679 classes, computing this for every class on every example would be very expensive for no benefit, since only the predicted-class figure is used below), then aggregate across examples.

```{python}
#| label: fig-labatt-corr-naf
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlation between label-attention weights and |Captum IG| scores at word level, for the predicted class. Left: overall distribution. Right: breakdown by predicted sub-class (top-20 most predicted)."

from scipy.stats import pearsonr, gaussian_kde
import pandas as pd

if not HAS_LAT_NAF:
    print("Label-attention artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    rows_naf = []
    n_ex_naf = min(len(cap_la["words"]), len(lat_la["words"]))
    for i in range(n_ex_naf):
        cap_mat = _class_sorted(cap_la, i)
        lat_mat = lat_la["word_attn"][i]
        nw = min(cap_mat.shape[1], lat_mat.shape[1])
        if nw < 3:
            continue
        y_pred_i = int(cap_la["y_pred"][i])
        y_true_i = int(cap_la["y_true"][i])
        ig = np.abs(cap_mat[y_pred_i, :nw])
        la = lat_mat[y_pred_i, :nw]
        if ig.std() < 1e-9 or la.std() < 1e-9:
            continue
        r, _ = pearsonr(la, ig)
        rows_naf.append({"r": float(r), "y_pred": y_pred_i, "y_true": y_true_i,
                          "correct": y_pred_i == y_true_i})
    pred_df_naf = pd.DataFrame(rows_naf)

    top_preds_naf = pred_df_naf["y_pred"].value_counts().head(20).index.tolist()

    fig_lc = make_subplots(
        rows=1, cols=2,
        subplot_titles=["Overall distribution", "By predicted sub-class (top-20)"],
        horizontal_spacing=0.12,
    )

    r_vals_naf = pred_df_naf["r"].dropna().values
    kde    = gaussian_kde(r_vals_naf, bw_method=0.25)
    x_grid = np.linspace(r_vals_naf.min() - 0.05, r_vals_naf.max() + 0.05, 300)
    kde_y  = kde(x_grid)
    bin_w  = (r_vals_naf.max() - r_vals_naf.min()) / 25
    fig_lc.add_trace(go.Histogram(
        x=r_vals_naf, nbinsx=25, marker_color="#1565C0", opacity=0.5, showlegend=False,
    ), row=1, col=1)
    fig_lc.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x_grid, y=kde_y * len(r_vals_naf) * bin_w,
        mode="lines", line=dict(color="#1565C0", width=2.5), showlegend=False,
    ), row=1, col=1)
    fig_lc.add_vline(x=r_vals_naf.mean(), line_dash="dash", line_color="#B71C1C",
                      annotation_text=f"mean={r_vals_naf.mean():.2f}",
                      annotation_position="top right", row=1, col=1)

    for c in top_preds_naf:
        sub = pred_df_naf[pred_df_naf["y_pred"] == c]["r"]
        fig_lc.add_trace(go.Box(
            y=sub, name=CLASS_CODE[c], marker_color=PALETTE[c],
            showlegend=False, boxpoints="outliers",
        ), row=1, col=2)

    fig_lc.update_xaxes(title_text="Pearson r", row=1, col=1)
    fig_lc.update_yaxes(title_text="Count", row=1, col=1)
    fig_lc.update_xaxes(tickangle=-45, tickfont=dict(size=9), row=1, col=2)
    fig_lc.update_yaxes(title_text="Pearson r", row=1, col=2)
    fig_lc.update_layout(height=450, template="plotly_white", margin=dict(t=50))
    fig_lc.show()
```

### Are these explanations faithful? A word-deletion stress test

Attribution scores are only meaningful if the model would *actually* change its mind were those words removed. We test this directly: progressively delete the words Captum ranked as most important for the predicted class, and watch how fast that class's predicted probability collapses. As a control, we delete the *same number* of **randomly chosen** words, averaged over 3 draws, isolating the effect of *which* words are removed from the trivial effect of mutilating the description.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-faithfulness-naf
#| fig-cap: "Faithfulness (comprehensiveness) test: mean probability retained by the originally-predicted class as the most-attributed words are progressively deleted (solid = guided removal by |Captum score|; dotted = random-removal control, averaged over 3 draws). Shaded bands show ±1 std across examples."

HAS_FAI_NAF = HAS_LA and all(FAITHFUL.get(k) is not None for k in MODEL_KEYS)

if not HAS_FAI_NAF:
    print("Faithfulness artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    fig_fai_naf = go.Figure()
    for key in MODEL_KEYS:
        fai   = FAITHFUL[key]
        fr    = fai["fractions"]
        color = "#1565C0" if key == "labatt" else "#B71C1C"
        rgb   = "21,101,192" if key == "labatt" else "183,28,28"
        for arr, name, dash in [(fai["guided_probs"], "guided removal", "solid"),
                                (fai["random_probs"], "random removal (control)", "dot")]:
            m, s = np.nanmean(arr, axis=0), np.nanstd(arr, axis=0)
            fig_fai_naf.add_trace(go.Scatter(
                x=np.concatenate([fr, fr[::-1]]), y=np.concatenate([m + s, (m - s)[::-1]]),
                fill="toself", fillcolor=f"rgba({rgb},0.10)", line=dict(width=0),
                mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
            ))
            fig_fai_naf.add_trace(go.Scatter(
                x=fr, y=m, mode="lines+markers", name=f"{MODEL_LABELS[key]} — {name}",
                line=dict(color=color, dash=dash, width=2.5), marker=dict(size=6, color=color),
            ))
    fig_fai_naf.update_layout(
        xaxis_title="Fraction of words removed",
        yaxis_title="Mean retained probability of the predicted class",
        yaxis_range=[0, 1.02], paper_bgcolor="white", plot_bgcolor="white",
        height=460, margin=dict(t=30, b=20, l=10, r=10),
        legend=dict(x=1.02, y=1, xanchor="left"),
    )
    fig_fai_naf.show()

    print("Faithfulness gap — area between the random and guided curves (higher = more faithful):\n")
    for key in MODEL_KEYS:
        fai = FAITHFUL[key]
        gap = float(np.trapezoid(np.nanmean(fai["random_probs"], 0) - np.nanmean(fai["guided_probs"], 0), fai["fractions"]))
        print(f"  {MODEL_LABELS[key]:<32} {gap:+.4f}")
```
